theorems.theorem_title: The Zipf p-series converges exactly for $s>1$
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipf_summable_iff (s : ℝ) (hs : 0 ≤ s) :
    Summable (fun k : ℕ => 1 / ((k : ℝ) + 1) ^ s) ↔ 1 < s := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement: For a real exponent $s\ge0$, the series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$ is summable if and only if $s>1$. This is the convergence criterion in the infinite-extension theorem, isolated for reuse in both its convergent and divergent branches.
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law, section "Formal definition"; auxiliary lemma for the original ZipfLaw mission, derived from its displayed PMF and generalized harmonic sum.

theorems.theorem_title: For $s>1$, the Zipf harmonic sums tend to $\zeta(s)$
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipf_genHarmonic_tendsto_zeta (s : ℝ) (hs : 1 < s) :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun N : ℕ => ((genHarmonic N s : ℝ) : ℂ)) Filter.atTop
      (nhds (riemannZeta s)) := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement: If $s>1$, the generalized harmonic partial sums $H_{N,s}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}k^{-s}$ converge to Riemann's zeta function $\zeta(s)$. The formal limit takes place in $\mathbb C$ after casting the real sums, because Mathlib's `riemannZeta` is complex-valued.
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law, section "Formal definition"; auxiliary lemma for the original ZipfLaw mission, derived from its displayed PMF and generalized harmonic sum.

theorems.theorem_title: For $0\le s\le1$, the Zipf harmonic sums tend to infinity
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipf_genHarmonic_tendsto_atTop (s : ℝ) (hs : 0 ≤ s) (hs1 : s ≤ 1) :
    Filter.Tendsto (fun N : ℕ => genHarmonic N s) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement: For every real exponent $0\le s\le1$, the generalized harmonic sums $H_{N,s}$ tend to $+\infty$ as $N\to\infty$. In particular no finite normalizing constant can extend these finite Zipf laws to infinitely many ranks.
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law, section "Formal definition"; auxiliary lemma for the original ZipfLaw mission, derived from its displayed PMF and generalized harmonic sum.

theorems.theorem_title: A nonempty generalized harmonic sum is positive
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem genHarmonic_pos (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N) (s : ℝ) : 0 < genHarmonic N s := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement: For every integer $N\ge1$ and real exponent $s$, the generalized harmonic sum $H_{N,s}=\sum_{k=1}^{N} k^{-s}$ is strictly positive. This ensures that the common normalizing factor can be cancelled and logarithms of supported Zipf probabilities are well-defined.
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law, section "Formal definition"; auxiliary lemma for the original ZipfLaw mission, derived from its displayed PMF and generalized harmonic sum.

theorems.theorem_title: All finite Zipf moments are ratios of shifted harmonic sums
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipfPMF_moment (N : ℕ) (s : ℝ) (p : ℕ) :
    (∑ k ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, (k : ℝ) ^ p * zipfPMF N s k) =
      genHarmonic N (s - p) / genHarmonic N s := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement: For every cutoff $N\in\mathbb N$, real exponent $s$, and integer moment order $p\ge0$, the finite Zipf law satisfies $\sum_{k=1}^{N} k^p f(k;s,N)=H_{N,s-p}/H_{N,s}$. The identity includes $N=0$ under Lean's convention for division by zero. The first and second moment formulas in the mission are its special cases.
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law, section "Formal definition"; auxiliary lemma for the original ZipfLaw mission, derived from its displayed PMF and generalized harmonic sum.

theorems.theorem_title: Zipf extends to infinitely many items iff $s>1$; then $H_{N,s}\to\zeta(s)$
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipf_infinite_extension (s : ℝ) (hs : 0 ≤ s) :
    (Summable (fun k : ℕ => 1 / ((k : ℝ) + 1) ^ s) ↔ 1 < s) ∧
      (1 < s → Filter.Tendsto (fun N : ℕ => ((genHarmonic N s : ℝ) : ℂ)) Filter.atTop
        (nhds (riemannZeta s))) ∧
      (s ≤ 1 → Filter.Tendsto (fun N : ℕ => genHarmonic N s) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop) := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law), snapshot uploaded by the proposer, section "Formal definition" ("The generalized Zipf distribution can be extended to infinitely many items (N = ∞) only if the exponent s exceeds 1. In that case, the normalization constant H_{N,s} becomes Riemann's zeta function ... If the exponent s is 1 or less, the normalization constant H_{N,s} diverges as N tends to infinity").

namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipfPMF_sum_eq_one (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N) (s : ℝ) :
    ∑ k ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, zipfPMF N s k = 1 := by sorry

theorems.natural_language_statement:
For every integer $N\ge1$ and real exponent $s$,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{N}f(k;N,s)=\sum_{k=1}^N\frac{1}{H_{N,s}\,k^s}=1 .$$

This is the statement that $H_{N,s}$ is the normalization constant of the Zipf distribution.

theorems.theorem_title: $f(1)/f(n)=n^s$: the top item is $n^s$ times as frequent as the $n$-th
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipfPMF_ratio (N : ℕ) (s : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (hn1 : 1 ≤ n) (hnN : n ≤ N) :
    zipfPMF N s 1 / zipfPMF N s n = (n : ℝ) ^ s := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement:
For $1\le n\le N$ and real $s$, the most probable item is exactly $n^s$ times as probable as the item of rank $n$:
$$\frac{f(1;N,s)}{f(n;N,s)}=n^{s}.$$
For $s=1$: the most common word occurs $n$ times as often as the $n$-th most common one.

theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem log_zipfPMF_affine (N : ℕ) (s : ℝ) (k : ℕ) (hk1 : 1 ≤ k) (hkN : k ≤ N) :
    Real.log (zipfPMF N s k) = -s * Real.log k - Real.log (genHarmonic N s) := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement:
For $1\le k\le N$ and real $s$,
$$\ln f(k;N,s)=-s\ln k-\ln H_{N,s},$$

theorems.formal_statement:

theorem zipfPMF_mode (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N) (s : ℝ) (hs : 0 ≤ s) (k : ℕ) :
    zipfPMF N s k ≤ zipfPMF N s 1 := by sorry

$$f(k;N,s)\le f(1;N,s)=\frac1{H_{N,s}}.$$

theorems.theorem_title: Zipf–Mandelbrot law with Hurwitz-zeta normalization is a distribution
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipfMandelbrotPMF_hasSum_one (q s : ℝ) (hq : 0 ≤ q) (hs : 1 < s) :
    HasSum (fun k : ℕ => zipfMandelbrotPMF q s k) 1 := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement:
Let $s>1$ and $q\ge0$. With normalizing constant $C=\zeta(s,q+1)=\sum_{k\ge1}(k+q)^{-s}$ (Hurwitz zeta), the Zipf–Mandelbrot frequencies
$$f(k;q,s)=\frac{1}{C}\,\frac{1}{(k+q)^s},\qquad k=1,2,3,\dots$$
form a probability distribution:
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}f(k;q,s)=1 .$$
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law), snapshot uploaded by the proposer, section "Related laws" ($f(k;N,q,s)=\frac1C\frac1{(k+q)^s}$; "The constant C is the Hurwitz zeta function evaluated at s").

theorems.theorem_title: Random typing produces a power law in rank (Li's model)
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem monkey_typing_power_law (m : ℕ) (hm : 2 ≤ m) (q : ℝ) (hq : 0 < q) (hmq : (m : ℝ) * q < 1)
    (e : ℕ → List (Fin m)) (he_inj : Function.Injective e)
    (he_range : Set.range e = {w | w ≠ []})
    (he_sorted : Antitone (fun r => monkeyWordProb m q (e r))) :
    ∃ C₁ C₂ : ℝ, 0 < C₁ ∧ 0 < C₂ ∧ ∀ r : ℕ,
      C₁ * ((r : ℝ) + 1) ^ (-Real.logb m (1 / q)) ≤ monkeyWordProb m q (e r) ∧
        monkeyWordProb m q (e r) ≤ C₂ * ((r : ℝ) + 1) ^ (-Real.logb m (1 / q)) := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement:
Consider a monkey typing on a keyboard with $m\ge2$ letter keys, each pressed with the same probability $q>0$, and a space bar pressed with probability $1-mq>0$. The probability that the word following a space is exactly the string $w$ of letters is $p(w)=q^{|w|}(1-mq)$. List all nonempty words in order of non-increasing probability, $w_1,w_2,w_3,\dots$ (ties in any order). Then the probability of the word of rank $r$ obeys a power law in $r$: with $\alpha=\log_m(1/q)$ there are constants $0<C_1\le C_2$ such that for all $r\ge1$
$$C_1\,r^{-\alpha}\le p(w_r)\le C_2\,r^{-\alpha}.$$

**Formalization Note.** Ranks are $0$-indexed in Lean: the rank order is a bijection $e:\mathbb N\to\{\text{nonempty words}\}$ along which $p$ is non-increasing, and the bound is stated with $(r+1)^{-\alpha}$.
theorems.source: Wikipedia, "Zipf's law" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law), snapshot uploaded by the proposer, section "Statistical explanations" (Li: "in a document in which each character has been chosen randomly from a uniform distribution of all letters (plus a space character), the 'words' with different lengths follow the macro-trend of Zipf's law"; ref. Li 1992, https://doi.org/10.1109/18.165464).

Let $m\ge2$ be a natural number, $q$ a real with $q>0$ and $mq<1$. Let $e$ be a function from $\mathbb N$ to finite lists over an $m$-letter alphabet which is injective, whose image is exactly the set of nonempty lists, and such that $r\mapsto q^{|e(r)|}(1-mq)$ is antitone (non-increasing in $r$). theorems.theorem_title: Leading digits of Zipf ($s=1$) data follow Benford's law
theorems.formal_statement:
namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipf_one_leadingDigit_benford (d : ℕ) (hd1 : 1 ≤ d) (hd9 : d ≤ 9) :
    Filter.Tendsto
      (fun N : ℕ => ∑ k ∈ (Finset.Icc 1 N).filter (fun k => leadingDigit k = d), zipfPMF N 1 k)
      Filter.atTop (nhds (Real.logb 10 (1 + 1 / (d : ℝ)))) := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement:
Let $K_N$ be a random rank drawn from the Zipf distribution with $s=1$ on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, $\mathbb P(K_N=k)=\frac{1}{H_N\,k}$. For every digit $d\in\{1,\dots,9\}$, the probability that the leading decimal digit of $K_N$ equals $d$ tends to the Benford probability:
$$\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le N\\ D_{10}(k)=d}}\frac{1}{H_N\,k}=\log_{10}\!\left(1+\frac1d\right).$$

**Formalization Note.** The source's sentence does not say which numbers' leading digits are meant; this item reads it as the leading digits of the ranks $k$ when $k$ occurs with Zipf ($s=1$) frequency $\propto 1/k$. (The other reading, the leading digits of the values $C/k$ for $k = 1, \dots, N$ counted once each, is the reciprocal sequence, which does not satisfy Benford's law.)

namespace ZipfLaw

theorem zipfPMF_cdf (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 ≤ N) (s : ℝ) (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≤ N) :
    ∑ k ∈ Finset.Icc 1 n, zipfPMF N s k = genHarmonic n s / genHarmonic N s := by sorry

end ZipfLaw
theorems.natural_language_statement:
For integers $N\ge1$, $0\le n\le N$ and real $s$, the cumulative distribution function of the Zipf distribution is
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(k;N,s)=\frac{H_{n,s}}{H_{N,s}} .$$
